label: data integrity and financial systems
overview: Data integrity and financial systems scenarios typically present as one of three underlying problems: the data itself is inaccurate or untimely (a systems or process issue); the client has the data but cannot interpret it correctly (a literacy and context issue); or the client is reacting to data in ways that create new problems (a volatility and judgement issue). The advisor's role is to diagnose which layer the problem sits in before recommending a tool. This domain holds four materials: the interpretive mindset that has to come first, the spreadsheet that standardises the numbers, the deck that sets the ground rules for comparing them, and the framework for running the ongoing review session.

diagnostic_entry.primary_question: Is the problem that the client cannot get clean, reliable data — or that they have data but do not know what to do with it?
diagnostic_entry.cannot_get_clean_data: Address the upstream system first — Chart of Accounts structure, bookkeeping processes, cloud accounting setup, or admin procedures. A reporting framework built on dirty data will compound the problem rather than solve it.
diagnostic_entry.has_data_but_cannot_interpret: Move to the materials below. Start with Deming's Theory of Volatility to establish the right interpretive mindset, then use Ratio Analysis or Dashboard Discussions depending on the depth of engagement required.

materials.name: Deming's Theory of Volatility
materials.summary: Moves the client from reacting to every movement in the numbers to reading them in context, replacing the average line — which makes each result an automatic pass or fail — with a standard deviation band showing the likely range. Volatility is expected and carries a degree of predictability; the work is to understand its nature, not fight it. It is a caravan swaying behind a car: control the sway before accelerating.
materials.who_when: Use before any reporting framework is introduced, with any client who reacts to single results — paying a bonus for one good month, cutting staff after one bad one, or blaming the team for swings outside their control — and with any client planning to grow.
steps: Plot the key metric — sales or cash received — and add standard deviation lines above and below it to establish the upper and lower likely range, instead of drawing an average line through the data.

Explain why the average fails as a performance measure: results naturally land above or below it, so every period becomes an automatic pass or fail. The standard deviation band instead shows where roughly 68% of results are expected to fall.
Open the conversation with the caravan metaphor, then ask: 'when you see your sales spike or drop, what do you typically do?' The answer surfaces whether the client is already tampering.

Read each movement against the four variation types — Common Cause (high frequency, low impact, such as a rainy day in retail; no management action required), Special Cause (low frequency, high impact, such as an earthquake or a pandemic; needs a genuine strategic response), Seasonal (predictable repeating patterns, such as ice cream in summer), and Tampering (acting on a misinterpretation, the most damaging of the four).

Ask the contextual questions of the data every time: is this consistent with our previous assumptions; do any of these points relate to a special or seasonal cause; are the swings being caused by our own campaigns? A furniture store's 'free Christmas ham' promotion may spike December while quietly cannibalising November and January.

Before acting on any anomaly, establish which relationship applies — Causation (a direct provable link: petrol in a diesel engine), Correlation (a highly attributable contribution: low tyre pressure and a pothole), or Coincidence (entirely unrelated: the music playing when the engine blew). Treating coincidence as causation is the most common form of tampering.

Name the tampering risk out loud: paying bonuses for a June spike and firing staff after a December trough, when both were the same predictable seasonal swing. The cost is invisible, because nobody ever learns what the right decision would have been.

Once the volatility is understood, apply the four options — review products and services to fill the holes in slow periods; review admin procedures to get the money in quicker; review marketing and sales tactics to attract more customers more often; review working capital, including retained earnings and overdraft facilities, to finance and manage the swings.

materials.name: Common Size Trend Analysis Template
materials.summary: A multi-tab spreadsheet holding up to six years of Profit & Loss and Balance Sheet actuals, converting raw dollars into common-size percentages — P&L against Total Sales, Balance Sheet against Total Assets — and calculating trend variations plus Activity, Profitability, Liquidity and Leverage ratios. Common sizing removes the distortion of revenue growth, so a year is judged on management decisions rather than the position it inherited. It is the defence against confirmation bias.
materials.who_when: Established businesses with several years of financial data that want to evaluate year-over-year operational trends, and advisors working the Compilation and Verification or Assimilation stages of the Advisory Staircase.
steps: Gather the client's verified Profit & Loss and Balance Sheet actuals for the number of years being reviewed, up to six.
Enter the raw financial figures into the clear and orange input boxes on the Profit & Loss and Balance Sheet tabs.

Review the automated common-size output — how each expense compares to Total Sales, and how each asset and liability class compares to Total Assets. This is the drag race correction: a car that starts ahead because of the last race may appear to win, and a year-on-year comparison without common sizing makes the same mistake.

Move to the Ratios tab and review the four families — Activity (such as Debtors Days on Hand), Profitability (such as Gross Margin), Liquidity, and Leverage. Every formula is defined on that tab, so the calculation can be checked rather than trusted: Return on Assets is (Net Profit + Bank Interest + Finance Interest) / Total Assets, and Return on Equity is Net Profit / Total Equity.
Scan the Trend columns for large percentage movements and use those as the shortlist for deeper investigation — the template identifies where to look, it does not explain why.
Work through the findings with the client rather than sending the finished sheet; a client who has handled the numbers assigns meaning to them, one who receives a completed report does not.

materials.name: Ratio Analysis Deck — the Advisory Staircase
materials.summary: The educational deck behind the numbers, setting out the five steps of the Advisory Staircase — Compilation and Verification, Assimilation, Interpretation, Application, Observation — and the ground rules for when data is and is not fair to compare. Its central discipline is Know Thyself First: quantify internal assumptions and build a predictive revenue model before buying any external benchmark. It holds a review to comparing apples with apples.
materials.who_when: Advisors running strategic planning or financial review sessions with owners who need to understand how to interpret and apply their own business data, and any client about to buy or rely on external benchmark data.
steps: Present the five components of business management so the client can see the journey the data takes: Compilation and Verification (collect it with integrity and timeliness), Assimilation (render it so it can be viewed and understood), Interpretation (separate correlation from causation, working together rather than handing over a finished report), Application (decide the next experiment and assign clear ownership), and Observation (review progress, learn, adapt, repeat).

Define the internal baseline first — build a predictive or scenario revenue model, validated against actual performance, before looking at any competitor. Buying external benchmark data before internal assumptions are captured and quantified is the rookie mistake.

Filter out the three conditions that make a comparison invalid: ratios calculated by different methods across periods; a one-off event distorting a period, such as a large order invoiced but unpaid inflating Debtors Days on Hand; and fundamentally different periods — compare peak to peak and low to low, never peak to low.

Interrogate any external benchmark before it is used: how many businesses does it cover, are they of similar size and structure, does it show upper and lower quartiles, how old is it, were the ratios calculated by identical methods, and are there geographical, seasonal or accounting differences that affect comparability.

Keep the assimilation stage deliberately manual — a shared spreadsheet the client helps populate rather than fully automated software. The tactile work is what creates understanding and ownership of the conclusion.

materials.name: Dashboard Discussions
materials.summary: Runs the monthly or quarterly dashboard review as a collaborative session rather than a report handover: the advisor challenges what the client believes to be true, the client explores with an open mind, and the objective is to discover what has been missed. Every metric is read through the 3x3 framework — Cause, Event and Effect against Do the Job, Get the Job and Get Organised — because the category determines which tactical levers are available. Seek information, not judgement.
materials.who_when: Ongoing monthly or quarterly reporting engagements, and particularly clients who already receive reports but do not act on them — the aim is to move the owner from passive recipient to active analyst. Requires data the client can already trust; fix the upstream system first if not.
steps: Set the objective and the mindset before any number is shown: the advisor is there to challenge what the client believes to be true, the client is there to explore issues and ideas with an open heart and an open mind, the objective is to discover what has been missed, and the session ends with recorded learnings and an action plan.

Map the metric to its 3x3 categories, because that is what determines the available levers. Do the Job — variable costs (materials, shipping, stock, contract labour, discounting) with levers in purchasing, warehousing and logistics efficiencies, project management, wastage and error reduction, and process or skill improvements. Get the Job — activity costs (general marketing and branding, salespeople on the road) with levers in product fit, positioning, packaging, pricing, bundling, message clarity, market knowledge, sales effectiveness, brand awareness and customer loyalty. Get Organised — fixed costs (the structural requirements to house staff and serve customers) with levers in use of assets, model design, management effectiveness, leadership, culture, employee engagement, strategic vision and stakeholder returns.

Work the standard dashboard metrics rather than one headline number: Sales to Gross Profit, Wages to Sales, Net Profit to Sales, Average Markup %, Working vs Fixed Capital, Quick Ratio and Days Trading Cover, Debt Ratio (assets vs liabilities), Debt to Shareholders Equity, Return on Equity, Division Wages %, Sales Mix by Margin, and a Volatility Analysis overlay.

Ask the same three questions of every metric: is this information consistent with your previous business assumptions and beliefs; which tactical options are of greatest influence and why; did you have any actions planned prior to this data, and do they still stand?

Hold the interpretation rules throughout — no single ratio or report gives the whole story, always define whether the data shows causation, correlation or coincidence, and always seek a balanced view by looking for both good and bad data.
Where a metric refuses to give up its meaning, run the 5 Whys — ask why five times, each answer forming the basis of the next question — until the root cause rather than the symptom is on the table.
Close by choosing the tactical options of greatest influence, recording what was learned, and documenting specific future action steps with owners, so the next session has something to observe.

advisor_guidance.sequencing: Introduce Deming's Theory of Volatility first — before any reporting framework — to establish the right interpretive mindset. If the client is reacting to data badly, no dashboard will help them until they understand variation. Ratio Analysis and Dashboard Discussions can then follow as the structured delivery vehicle.
advisor_guidance.dirty_data_first: If the client cannot generate reliable data in the first place, fix the upstream problem before introducing any reporting framework. A sophisticated dashboard built on inaccurate or incomplete data is worse than no dashboard — it creates false confidence.
advisor_guidance.collaborative_not_transactional: The biggest mistake advisors make with reporting is delivering a finished report and expecting the client to act on it. The client must be a participant in building the picture — not a passive recipient. Manual tools, joint sessions, and tactile engagement are what create understanding and ownership.
advisor_guidance.tampering_is_the_hidden_cost: When clients misinterpret data and take wrong action, the cost is invisible — they never know what the correct decision would have been. Tampering compounds on itself. Use Deming's framework to surface whether the client is already doing this before designing a reporting solution.
